speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: Sure. Well, the House Democracy Partnership has somewhat different historical origins. It goes back to this kind of effort, member to member, staff to staff this kind of effort to focus as colleagues on parliamentary effectiveness and to work with the parliament's in emerging democracy situations to increase the effectiveness of their institutions. This dates back to Eastern and Central Europe in the early 90s when communism was falling and the Soviet Union was dissolving. All kinds of countries had to take showcase parliaments and actually make them work. And colleague of mine, Martin Frost of Texas had a great idea back then that we should reach out in quite direct ways. Member to member staff to staff to help bring these parliaments along. And the effort back then focused very heavily on research capacity, libraries, IT, But our staff went over for weeks at a time to work and getting those parliaments up and running. And we made a lot of visits ourselves. And I was a very junior member at that point. And that left a very lasting impression on me. New Gingrich let the whole thing expire when he came in in the mid-90s. So I tried for years to get this back up and running. And finally succeeded 15 years ago with the help of Republican Speaker Dennis Haster. And he appointed David Dreyer to chair the commission that I became chairman when Democrats took over in, you know, in 2007. And we've maintained a back part as an effort ever since. We still have a lot of focus on Eastern and Central Europe. We work, for example, in Macedonia, Kosovo, Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine. But we also have a worldwide focus with countries like Indonesia and Kenya and Peru, countries that are, yes, they're struggling, but they've also shown a real commitment and a real capacity to become functioning representative democracies. And we think that they and we have a mutual stake in making sure that that works. We have a mantra that Yes, democracy is about free and fair elections. But what happens between elections is really maybe what will matter in a lot of cases. And in that period between elections, that's when representative institutions either work or they don't. And the result of their efforts make a huge difference for whether democracy takes over.
